query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Trace microalloying with a small amount (~0.5 at%) of zirconium (Zr) will promote the in situ formation of nanoscale, Zr‐rich dispersoids at lamellar colony interfaces in the eutectic HEA, thereby refining the lamellar spacing and strengthening the interfacial cohesion to both delay microcrack initiation and enhance back‐stress effects during deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: A eutectic high-entropy alloy (AlCoCrFeNi2.1 system) featuring dual-phase lamellar colonies with internal boundaries that serve as nucleation sites for microcracks during room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Introduce ~0.5 atomic percent Zr during the alloy melting stage.
generation.conditions: The processing route (melting, suction casting, and hybrid rolling) must be controlled so that Zr is initially dissolved and then segregates during solidification and thermomechanical processing into nanoscale dispersoids without forming coarse or brittle intermetallic phases. The dual-phase L12+B2 lamellar architecture must be retained.
generation.structural_mediator: The nanoscale Zr-rich dispersoids precipitate preferentially along the lamellar interfaces, resulting in a refined, more continuous interfacial network that pins grain boundaries and suppresses local stress concentrations.
generation.mechanism: By restraining interface mobility and limiting microcrack nucleation at the colony boundaries, the dispersoids enhance the accumulation of geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) during deformation. This leads to increased long-range back-stress strengthening while preserving ductility by delaying crack propagation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified alloy, the Zr-added alloy is expected to show a moderate increase in yield and ultimate tensile strengths (tentatively on the order of 10–20% improvement) along with higher uniform elongation owing to reduced microcrack formation.
generation.baseline: Unmodified eutectic HEA produced via conventional suction casting and hybrid rolling with approximately 2000 MPa UTS and 8% uniform elongation.
generation.boundary: This intervention is effective only if the Zr addition results in the formation of fine, coherent dispersoids; excessive Zr or non-optimal processing could lead to coarse, brittle intermetallic phases that would be deleterious.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in mechanical properties is uncertain until thermodynamic and kinetic assessments (e.g., CALPHAD studies) confirm that Zr segregates as intended without adversely altering phase stability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one with standard composition and one with ~0.5 at% Zr added. Process both batches identically by suction casting followed by hybrid rolling. Use TEM coupled with EDS mapping to identify the presence and distribution of nanoscale Zr-rich dispersoids at colony interfaces, and then perform room-temperature tensile tests.
measurements: Yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and uniform elongation from tensile tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Zr-added samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in both strength and ductility, or if microstructural analysis fails to reveal the formation of fine Zr-rich dispersoids at targeted interfaces, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: A second tunable strengthening mechanism of eutectic structures is the spacing of the secondary phase. By changing the spacing of the secondary phase, the fraction of contact between the two phases through shared phase boundaries is also changed. By decreasing the spacing of the eutectic phase, creating a fine eutectic structure, more surface area is shared between the two constituent phases resulting in more effective load transfer. On the micro-scale, the additional boundary area acts as a barrier to dislocations further strengthening the material. As a result of this strengthening mechanism, coarse eutectic structures tend to be less stiff but more ductile while fine eutectic structures are stiffer but more brittle. The spacing of the eutectic phase can be controlled during processing as it is directly related to the cooling rate during solidification of the eutectic structure. top3.what_is_new: Unlike the paper’s processing‐only approach, this proposal introduces a compositional intervention (trace Zr addition) to specifically tailor interfacial structures and reinforce colony boundaries—a strategy not previously investigated in the reference work.

top3.builds_on: the finding of a hierarchically decomposed nano-lamellar structure in the paper (PMC7075928) confirming that phase morphology and interfacial features critically affect strength-toughness trade-offs.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a cyclic thermal processing intervention (instead of a single anneal) to actively modify interlamellar boundaries and precipitate distribution to alleviate microcracking, a processing strategy not explored in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: Introducing a cyclic heat‐treatment (temperature cycling) step after cold-rolling can further refine and stabilize the nano-lamellar eutectoid microstructure, strengthening interlamellar interfaces and reducing microcrack initiation to simultaneously improve strength and room-temperature tensile ductility.
fields.material_initial_state: Al0.3CoFeNi processed into dual-phase lamellar colonies via cold-rolling followed by a single isothermal anneal at 600 °C (CRSA600 baseline) or 700 °C (CRSA700/CR700 conditions).
fields.intervention: Apply a cyclic annealing treatment (e.g., alternating between 600 °C and a lower temperature such as 500–550 °C) following cold rolling.
fields.conditions: Maintain the same alloy composition and initial severe plastic deformation (e.g., 85% reduction); use multiple short annealing steps (e.g., 1–2 hrs at high temperature followed by controlled cooling to a lower annealing step, repeated for several cycles) designed to relieve interfacial residual stresses and promote a graded evolution of precipitates.
fields.structural_mediator: A more refined and homogeneous distribution of nano-scale precipitates and improved continuity at interlamellar boundaries, reducing stress concentration sites.
fields.mechanism: Cyclic treatments can allow partial decomposition and re-distribution of both L12 and B2 phases while healing residual stresses at internal boundaries. The cycling relieves localized stresses and permits gradual reorganization of precipitates, enhancing interface cohesion and rendering the lamellar colonies less susceptible to microcracking. Similar strategies have improved mechanical properties in steel pearlite via lamellar spacing refinement and stress relaxation (see TXT::wikipedia::Eutectic_system::012 and TXT::wikipedia::Ductility::003 for analogous effects in eutectic systems).
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified lamellar baseline, an increase in yield strength (potentially similar or modestly higher than the ~1074 MPa range) along with a significant improvement in tensile ductility (exceeding the 8% ductility of CRSA600 and potentially approaching or exceeding 20% ductility).
fields.baseline: The CRSA600 condition with a static 600 °C anneal that produces a hierarchical nano-lamellar structure with ~8% ductility.
fields.boundary: The benefits are expected only if the cyclic annealing parameters (temperature range, hold time, and cooling rate) are optimized to avoid over-coarsening of precipitates or excessive recovery that would remove strengthening features.
fields.uncertainty: Precise quantitative improvements in strength and ductility depend on the exact thermal cycle parameters, and the optimum cycle window is not predetermined.

measurements: Characterize the lamellar microstructure by TEM/SEM for precipitate size, interlamellar spacing, and interfacial integrity.
Perform tensile tests at room temperature to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cyclic annealed samples do not show a statistically significant (beyond experimental error) improvement in both strength and ductility compared to the baseline, or if the microstructure shows signs of detrimental coarsening or increased interfacial cracking, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

top3.builds_on: The mechanism of accelerating heterogeneous precipitation and formation of a refined, dual-domain microstructure observed in cryo-rolled CoCrFeNi2.1Nb0.2 HEA (PMC7142141) is extended to the eutectic HEA system.
top3.what_is_new: While the paper used cryo-rolling in a homogenized HEA with intermetallic precipitates, this hypothesis applies cryogenic deformation to eutectic dual-phase lamellar colonies to modify internal boundary characteristics and mitigate microcracking under tension.

fields.hypothesis: Introducing a cryogenic deformation step (cryo-rolling) in the processing of dual‐phase lamellar eutectic HEAs will induce a heterogeneous, refined microstructure that suppresses microcrack initiation while enhancing both strength and ductility.
fields.material_initial_state: Eutectic HEAs with dual‐phase lamellar colonies that exhibit coarse interlamellar spacing and internal boundaries susceptible to microcracking at room temperature.
fields.intervention: Apply severe cryogenic rolling (with ~90% thickness reduction) prior to conventional annealing.
fields.conditions: Specimens immersed in liquid nitrogen before and after each pass; subsequent annealing at a temperature similar to that in the paper (e.g., 800 °C/1 h) to trigger controlled precipitation.
fields.structural_mediator: Enhanced fragmentation of lamellar colonies, increased density of dislocations and internal boundaries, and accelerated nano-precipitate formation at interphase boundaries resulting in heterogeneous microstructural domains.
fields.mechanism: Cryogenic deformation increases stored energy and dislocation density, preferentially enhances precipitation kinetics at internal boundaries (via heterogeneous nucleation similar to the effect observed in the CoCrFeNi2.1Nb0.2 HEA in PMC7142141), which retards full recrystallization. This leads to coexisting deformed and recrystallized regions. The resulting geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) pile up at the boundaries, creating back stresses that delay crack initiation and promote uniform plasticity across both phases.
fields.predicted_outcome: Both yield strength and room-temperature tensile ductility will increase relative to conventional processed lamellar HEAs; expected improvements are qualitatively similar to the ~58% YS increase and slight ductility enhancement observed in the cryo-rolled CoCrFeNi2.1Nb0.2 alloy, though quantitative predictions in eutectic HEAs remain uncertain.
fields.baseline: Unmodified lamellar-colony eutectic HEAs processed by conventional room-temperature rolling and annealing that display limited ductility due to early microcrack initiation.
fields.boundary: The intervention is applicable as long as the alloy’s intrinsic phase stability is maintained during severe deformation and the annealing protocol allows controlled heterogeneous precipitation. Extreme alloy compositions or processing conditions that trigger disordering could invalidate this approach.
fields.uncertainty: The magnitude of enhancement in ductility and strength in eutectic HEAs may depend sensitively on the initial lamellar spacing and the alloy’s specific thermodynamics; precise quantitative effects remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples: one processed with conventional room-temperature rolling followed by annealing and another subjected to cryo-rolling (with liquid N2 immersion) with similar annealing treatment. Tensile specimens prepared identically will be tested at room temperature.
measurements: Fractography to assess microcrack initiation sites
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cryo-rolled samples do not exhibit statistically significant increases in both yield strength and ductility (or if they show reduced ductility due to premature failure), the hypothesis is falsified.
